lessons.title: Counting
lessons.objective: Connect a number word to a quantity; count on, compare, and recognize zero.
lessons.takeaway: Count each object once; the last count names the quantity.
lessons.scope: Counting, conservation of quantity, and counting on.

practice.prompt: Count the symbols ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● and explain your method.
practice.answer: Eight; pair each symbol with one count, without skipping or counting twice.

practice.prompt: Start with thirteen buttons and add three. Count on aloud and give the total.
practice.answer: Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen; total sixteen.

practice.prompt: You rearrange fourteen stones from a row into two piles. Explain why the total is unchanged.
practice.answer: No stone was added or removed. Regrouping changes positions but not the fourteen-object collection.

lessons.title: Place value
lessons.objective: Build and regroup whole numbers using powers of ten.
lessons.takeaway: Place value names the size of each counted bundle.
lessons.scope: Base-ten positions, equivalent regrouping, and multiplication by ten.

practice.prompt: What is the value of the digit three in three hundred sixty eight? Explain using bundles.
practice.answer: Three hundreds, so its value is 300.

practice.prompt: Represent fifty seven as four tens and some ones. How many ones are needed?
practice.answer: Seventeen ones: 40+17=57.

practice.prompt: Why does multiplying 206 by ten give 2060? Describe what happens to each nonzero digit.
practice.answer: Two hundreds become two thousands and six ones become six tens; 206×10=2060.

lessons.title: Addition and subtraction
lessons.objective: Combine quantities, find differences, and use inverse operations.
lessons.takeaway: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations on quantities.
lessons.scope: Combining, missing addends, decomposing numbers, and checking.

practice.prompt: Find eight plus five using a make-ten step.
Find forty seven plus thirty six by splitting one addend.
A store had ninety four notebooks and sold fifty eight. Find the remainder and check with addition.

lessons.title: Multiplication and division
lessons.objective: Connect equal groups, arrays, sharing, and remainders.
lessons.takeaway: Division reverses equal grouping; context determines how a remainder is used.
lessons.scope: Equal groups, arrays, quotients, and interpreted remainders.

practice.prompt: Draw four equal groups of six and find their total.
practice.answer: Four groups contain 24 objects: 4×6=24.

practice.prompt: Divide twenty nine objects into groups of four. State the quotient and remainder.
practice.answer: 29=4×7+1, so quotient 7 and remainder 1.

practice.prompt: Each boat holds seven passengers. How many boats are needed for thirty people, and why?
practice.answer: Five boats: four hold only 28, while five can hold all thirty.

lessons.title: Order of operations
lessons.objective: Read expression structure and evaluate grouped operations consistently.
lessons.takeaway: Grouping determines meaning; equal-priority operations proceed left to right.
lessons.scope: Expression structure, parentheses, powers, and equal-priority operations.

practice.prompt: Evaluate 7+4×3 and explain the first operation.
practice.answer: Multiplication first: 4×3=12, then 7+12=19.

practice.prompt: Evaluate 42÷7×3 using the equal-priority rule.
practice.answer: Left to right: 42÷7=6, then 6×3=18.

practice.prompt: Insert parentheses into 6+2×5 to make its value forty. Explain the new grouping.
practice.answer: (6+2)×5=40; the sum of eight is now the factor multiplied by five.

lessons.title: Estimation
lessons.objective: Round and bound quantities to check reasonableness before exact calculation.
lessons.takeaway: An estimate checks scale; explicit bounds state what is guaranteed.
lessons.scope: Rounding, compensation, multiplication estimates, and positive-factor bounds.

practice.prompt: Estimate 297+506 using convenient hundreds.
practice.answer: About 800, using 300+500.

practice.prompt: Estimate 48×21, then calculate exactly and compare.
practice.answer: Estimate 50×20=1000; exact value 1008, only eight larger.

practice.prompt: A calculation of 39×62 gives 24180. Explain without long multiplication why this is unreasonable.
practice.answer: 40×60 is about 2400; 24180 is roughly ten times too large. The exact value is 2418.

lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.objective: Interpret units and equivalence; add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions.
lessons.takeaway: Addition combines equal units; multiplication takes a part; division counts units.
lessons.scope: Fraction meaning, equivalence, operations, and a nonzero divisor.

practice.prompt: Find 1/5+1/2 using equal-sized pieces.
Find 3/5 of 5/8. Show how factors simplify.
practice.answer: (3/5)(5/8)=3/8, cancelling the common nonzero factor five.

practice.prompt: A 5/3-meter ribbon is cut into pieces of length 2/9 meter. How many complete pieces fit, and why?
practice.answer: (5/3)/(2/9)=15/2=7.5, so seven complete pieces fit; a partial eighth is not a complete piece.

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.objective: Relate decimal place value to fractions and perform decimal operations.
lessons.takeaway: Decimal digits count tenths, hundredths, and further powers of ten.
lessons.scope: Decimal place value, comparison, addition, and multiplication meaning.

practice.prompt: Which is larger, 0.56 or 0.6? Explain with hundredths.
Calculate 2.08+0.7 and show place-value alignment.
Explain why 0.2×0.7 is 0.14 rather than 1.4.
practice.answer: Two tenths times seven tenths is fourteen hundredths: (2/10)(7/10)=14/100.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.objective: Relate percent, fraction, and decimal; solve increase and decrease problems.
lessons.takeaway: A percentage change compares its difference with a specified starting whole.
lessons.scope: Percent equivalence, parts of a whole, and changing percentage bases.

practice.prompt: Find thirty percent of ninety and identify the whole.
practice.answer: 0.30×90=27; the whole is ninety.

practice.prompt: A price of eighty five increases by twenty percent. Find the new price.
A count rises from seventy five to ninety. Find its percentage increase and explain the denominator.
practice.answer: The increase is fifteen; 15/75=20%. The original seventy five is the comparison whole.

lessons.title: Ratios
lessons.objective: Compare quantities multiplicatively and distinguish part-to-part from part-to-whole.
lessons.takeaway: Name the two quantities and preserve their order before using a ratio.
lessons.scope: Part-to-part, part-to-whole, equivalent ratios, and unit rates.

practice.prompt: A group has three green counters and five orange counters. Give green-to-orange and green-to-total ratios.
practice.answer: Green:orange is 3:5; green:total is 3:8.

practice.prompt: A recipe uses four cups of water for three cups of rice. How much water for nine cups of rice?
practice.answer: Scale both quantities by three: twelve cups of water.

practice.prompt: Explain why a blue-to-white ratio of five to two does not mean five sevenths is the blue-to-white ratio.
practice.answer: Five sevenths is the blue-to-total fraction. Blue-to-white remains 5:2 because the comparison denominator is the white amount.

lessons.title: Proportions
lessons.objective: Use equivalent ratios and units to solve scaling problems.
lessons.takeaway: Proportional relationships have a constant ratio and scale together.
lessons.scope: Scaling, denominator clearing, and recognizing nonproportional fees.

practice.prompt: Five meters of fabric cost twenty dollars. At the same rate, what do eight meters cost?
practice.answer: The unit rate is four dollars per meter, so eight meters cost thirty two dollars.

practice.prompt: Solve 7/3=x/12 and justify the scaling.
practice.answer: The denominator multiplies by four, so x=28.

practice.prompt: A taxi charges three dollars plus two dollars per mile. Is total cost proportional to distance? Explain.
practice.answer: No. The fixed charge means zero miles still costs three dollars and cost per mile is not constant.

lessons.title: Negative numbers
lessons.objective: Interpret signed values, subtraction, products, and distances on a number line.
lessons.takeaway: Addition follows signed movement; subtraction adds the opposite.
lessons.scope: Signed positions, subtraction, distribution, and product signs.

practice.prompt: Compute −5+12 and describe the motion.
practice.answer: Start at negative five and move twelve right, reaching seven.

practice.prompt: Compute −9−(−6) and explain why.
practice.answer: Subtracting negative six adds six: −9+6=−3.

practice.prompt: Compare −5² with (−5)² and explain the role of parentheses.
practice.answer: −5²=−25 because the square acts on five first; (−5)²=25 because the negative number is the base.

lessons.title: Exponents
lessons.objective: Explain whole, zero, and negative powers through repeated multiplication.
lessons.takeaway: Exponent rules describe factor structure; zero and negative powers need a nonzero base.
lessons.scope: Repeated factors, exponent laws, reciprocals, and sum/product distinctions.

practice.prompt: Evaluate 3⁵ by repeated multiplication.
For a≠0, simplify a⁶/a² and a⁻³.
practice.answer: a⁶/a²=a⁴; a⁻³=1/a³.

practice.prompt: Explain why (p+q)² is not generally p²+q².
practice.answer: Multiplying (p+q)(p+q) produces p²+pq+qp+q², including two cross terms.

lessons.title: Roots
lessons.objective: Connect roots to powers and distinguish principal roots from equation solutions.
lessons.takeaway: Principal square roots are nonnegative; squared equations may have two solutions.
lessons.scope: Principal roots, equation solutions, product simplification, and absolute value.

practice.prompt: Evaluate √169 and state why its sign is fixed.
practice.answer: The principal square root is thirteen, the nonnegative number whose square is 169.

practice.prompt: Simplify √27 by identifying a perfect-square factor.
For t=−8, compare √(t²) with t. Explain the general rule.
practice.answer: √64=8, whereas t=−8. In general √(t²)=|t|.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.objective: Use symbols to name changing quantities and fixed unknowns.
lessons.takeaway: A variable names a quantity; its context supplies units and allowed values.
lessons.scope: Variables as inputs and unknowns, substitution, and contextual domains.

practice.prompt: Let b be the number of boxes, each containing eight pencils. Write a rule for the pencil count p.
practice.answer: p=8b, where b is a nonnegative whole-number count.

practice.prompt: Use p=8b to find p when b=6.
practice.answer: p=8×6=48 pencils.

practice.prompt: Using the same rule, a shipment contains eighty eight pencils. Find b and explain why 2.5 is not an allowed box count here.
practice.answer: b=88/8=11; the situation counts complete boxes, so fractional counts are excluded.

lessons.title: Expressions and the distributive property
lessons.objective: Identify terms and factors; distribute and combine like terms without changing value.
lessons.takeaway: Rewrite structure with distribution and like terms; expressions need not be equations.
lessons.scope: Expressions, distribution, like terms, and a leading negative sign.

practice.prompt: Expand 4(t+5), explaining each product.
practice.answer: 4t+20; four multiplies both t and five.

practice.prompt: Simplify 3(2x+1)+2x and name the like terms.
practice.answer: 6x+3+2x=8x+3; 6x and 2x are like terms.

practice.prompt: Explain why 8−(y−2) becomes 10−y rather than 6−y.
practice.answer: The negative sign distributes: 8−y+2=10−y.

lessons.title: One-step equations
lessons.objective: Preserve equality with inverse operations and check a solution.
lessons.takeaway: Undo an operation on both sides with a valid inverse operation.
lessons.scope: Equality preservation, inverse operations, verification, and zero multipliers.

practice.prompt: Solve z−7=16 and check the original equation.
Solve 6q=42 and state the inverse operation.
practice.answer: Divide both sides by six: q=7.

practice.prompt: Compare 0x=0 with 0x=8. How many real solutions does each have?
practice.answer: 0x=0 is true for all real x; 0x=8 has no real solution. Division by zero is never a valid solving step.

lessons.title: Multi-step equations
lessons.objective: Distribute, combine, and solve while preserving both sides of an equation.
lessons.takeaway: Each step rewrites a side or applies the same valid operation to both sides.
lessons.scope: Distribution, collecting unknowns, inverse steps, and original-equation checks.

practice.prompt: Solve 3r+2=29, showing each operation on both sides.
practice.answer: Subtract two: 3r=27. Divide by three: r=9.

practice.prompt: Solve 4(t+2)=2t+22 and check.
practice.answer: 4t+8=2t+22; 2t=14; t=7. Both original sides equal36.

practice.prompt: Explain why subtracting 2x from both sides is valid in 5x−1=2x+14, then solve it.
practice.answer: Subtracting equal quantities preserves equality: 3x−1=14, so x=5.

lessons.title: Inequalities
lessons.objective: Represent comparison, solve one-variable inequalities, and interpret boundary points.
lessons.takeaway: Inequalities describe sets; negative scaling reverses their order.
lessons.scope: Strict and inclusive boundaries, interval meaning, and negative division.

practice.prompt: Solve y+7≤11 and describe the boundary point.
practice.answer: y≤4; the boundary four is included.

practice.prompt: Solve −3u≥12 and explain the changed sign.
practice.answer: Divide by negative three and reverse the comparison: u≤−4.

practice.prompt: Test one allowed and one excluded value for 2t−1>9.
practice.answer: t>5. For example, t=6 gives11>9; t=5 gives9>9, which is false.

lessons.title: Coordinate plane
lessons.objective: Locate ordered pairs and read axes, scales, and signed changes.
lessons.takeaway: Coordinate order and axis scales determine a point; coordinate differences describe displacement.
lessons.scope: Ordered pairs, signed coordinates, differences, and constant-coordinate lines.

practice.prompt: Plot or describe the point (−3,−1) from the origin.
practice.answer: Move three units left and one unit down.

practice.prompt: Find the horizontal and vertical changes from (−1,−2) to (4,3).
Describe all points with x=−2. Explain why this is a vertical line.
practice.answer: Every point has form (−2,y): horizontal position stays fixed while height varies, creating a vertical line.

lessons.title: Basic functions
lessons.objective: Distinguish an input, an output, and an equation to solve; substitute whole expressions.
lessons.takeaway: Distinguish supplying an input, substituting an expression, and solving for an input.
lessons.scope: Input-output meaning, whole-expression substitution, and inverse questions.

practice.prompt: For f(x)=2x−7, find f(6) and identify input and output.
practice.answer: f(6)=5; input six and output five.

practice.prompt: For f(x)=2x−7, simplify f(s+4).
For the same rule, solve f(x)=15. Explain how this differs from evaluating f(15).
practice.answer: 2x−7=15 gives x=11. Evaluating f(15) instead supplies input fifteen and gives output23.

lessons.title: Word problems
lessons.objective: Name quantities, track units, build a model, and check its interpretation.
lessons.takeaway: Name quantities and units, model the relationship, solve, then check the context.
lessons.scope: Linear word models, fixed and variable contributions, and feasibility.

practice.prompt: A bicycle rental charges six dollars plus three per hour. Write a cost rule and define its variables.
practice.answer: C=6+3h, with h rental hours and C total dollars.

practice.prompt: Using that rental rule, find the cost for five hours.
practice.answer: 6+3×5=21 dollars.

practice.prompt: A bill under the same rule is thirty dollars. Find the rental duration and check its units.
practice.answer: 6+3h=30 gives h=8 hours. The distance between thirty and the fixed fee is24 dollars, divided by3 dollars per hour.

lessons.title: Linear equations
lessons.objective: Relate slope-intercept forms and solve linear models.
lessons.takeaway: Equivalent linear equations describe the same satisfying points.
lessons.scope: Linear forms, fixed-output solving, and horizontal special cases.

practice.prompt: For y=4x−2, find the point whose input is three.
practice.answer: y=4×3−2=10, so the point is (3,10).

practice.prompt: Rewrite 3x−y=8 with y isolated, and find its vertical intercept.
practice.answer: y=3x−8; vertical intercept (0,−8).

practice.prompt: Explain why y=−4 has infinitely many ordered-pair solutions but 2x+1=7 has one real x solution.
practice.answer: The first permits every x with fixed y=−4; the second constrains one variable to x=3.

lessons.title: Linear inequalities
lessons.objective: Solve and graph linear constraints, reversing order when multiplying by negatives.
lessons.takeaway: Combine constraints by intersecting their solution sets, then apply the context.
lessons.scope: Compound linear constraints, endpoints, and discrete feasible values.

practice.prompt: Solve 5x+4≤29 over the real numbers.
practice.answer: Subtract four and divide by five: x≤5.

practice.prompt: Combine x>−1 with x≤6 and describe both endpoints.
practice.answer: −1<x≤6; negative one is excluded and six is included.

practice.prompt: A club needs at least three vans. Each van costs forty dollars and the budget is two hundred ten. List feasible whole van counts.
practice.answer: n≥3 and40n≤210 give3≤n≤5.25; whole feasible counts are3,4,5.

lessons.title: Systems of equations
lessons.objective: Solve simultaneous equations by intersection, substitution, and elimination.
lessons.takeaway: A system requires simultaneous truth; intersections determine its solution set.
lessons.scope: Substitution, shared solutions, parallel lines, and dependent equations.

practice.prompt: Solve y=x+2 and y=4x−7, then check both.
practice.answer: x+2=4x−7 gives x=3, y=5; both rules give five.

practice.prompt: Solve x+y=11 and x−y=3 using addition.
practice.answer: Add equations to get2x=14, sox=7; theny=4.

practice.prompt: Classify y=−3x+2 and 2y=−6x+4. Explain the geometry.
practice.answer: Infinitely many solutions; dividing the second equation by two gives the first, so both describe one line.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.objective: Connect domains, ranges, tables, formulas, and graphs.
lessons.takeaway: A function needs one output per allowed input; domain and range play different roles.
lessons.scope: Function criteria, domains, ranges, and the vertical-line test.

practice.prompt: For f(x)=(x−2)², can two different real inputs share an output? Give an example.
practice.answer: Yes. Inputs one and three both produce one; each input still has just one output.

practice.prompt: State the real domain of h(x)=1/(x+7), with a reason.
practice.answer: All real x except−7, because the denominator must be nonzero.

practice.prompt: Does x=y²+1 define y as a function of x over its full relation? Justify with one input.
practice.answer: No. At x=5, both y=2 and y=−2 satisfy the relation.

lessons.title: Slope
lessons.objective: Interpret rise over run as a signed rate with meaningful units.
lessons.takeaway: Slope is a signed rate, with a nonzero horizontal change and meaningful units.
lessons.scope: Rate, consistent subtraction, negative slope, and vertical/horizontal distinctions.

practice.prompt: Find the slope through (1,2) and (5,14), showing both changes.
practice.answer: Δy=12, Δx=4, so slope3.

practice.prompt: Find the slope through (−2,6) and (4,0).
A graph shows meters vertically and seconds horizontally. Explain the units of slope and the difference between zero and undefined slope.
practice.answer: Slope has meters per second. Zero slope means no vertical change; undefined slope occurs for zero horizontal change with distinct points.

lessons.title: Graphing
lessons.objective: Translate linear relationships between equations, tables, and graphs.
lessons.takeaway: A graph represents every valid pair, not just a table of sampled points.
lessons.scope: Tables, linear graphs, intercepts, and recognizing nonlinear structure.

practice.prompt: Make a three-point table and sketch y=3x−2 using inputs zero, one, and two.
practice.answer: The points are(0,−2),(1,1),(2,4); draw the straight line through them.

practice.prompt: Find both intercepts of y=−4x+8.
practice.answer: Vertical intercept(0,8); horizontal intercept(2,0).

practice.prompt: Why do three points from y=x² not justify replacing the whole graph with a straight line?
practice.answer: The rule is nonlinear: slopes change with x. Samples must be interpreted using the equation, which defines a parabola.

lessons.title: Polynomials and binomial expansion
lessons.objective: Multiply every term by every term and recognize the middle term of a square.
lessons.takeaway: Distribute every factor to every term; common factors enable valid simplification.
lessons.scope: Binomial products, cross terms, and difference-quotient preparation.

practice.prompt: Expand (u+5)² and identify both cross products.
Expand (2t+1)(t+4), showing every product.
For h≠0, simplify ((7+h)²−49)/h and explain why division is valid.
practice.answer: The numerator is14h+h²=h(14+h), so the quotient is14+h when h≠0.

lessons.title: Factoring
lessons.objective: Reverse distribution, identify common factors, and factor differences of squares.
lessons.takeaway: Factoring exposes products for zero equations and cancellation, while restrictions remain.
lessons.scope: Common factors, quadratic factoring, zero products, and rational restrictions.

practice.prompt: Factor 12z²+18z and verify by expanding.
practice.answer: 6z(2z+3), which expands to12z²+18z.

practice.prompt: Factor t²+8t+15 and solve when this expression equals zero.
practice.answer: (t+3)(t+5), givingt=−3 or−5.

practice.prompt: Simplify (x²−64)/(x−8), preserving the original restriction.
practice.answer: (x−8)(x+8)/(x−8)=x+8 for x≠8. The original function is still undefined at eight.

lessons.title: Quadratics
lessons.objective: Connect factored forms, roots, graphs, and the zero-product property.
lessons.takeaway: Equivalent quadratic forms reveal roots, turning points, and symmetric solutions.
lessons.scope: Factored and vertex forms, completing the square, and both square-root signs.

practice.prompt: Solve x²−6x+8=0 by factoring.
Write x²+8x+11 in completed-square form and identify its vertex.
practice.answer: (x+4)²−5, with vertex(−4,−5).

practice.prompt: Solve (t+2)²=9 and explain why one sign is not enough.
practice.answer: t+2=±3 gives t=1 or−5; both positive and negative three square to nine.

lessons.title: Exponential functions
lessons.objective: Recognize constant ratios and compare exponential with linear growth.
lessons.takeaway: Exponential models have a constant ratio; linear models have a constant difference.
lessons.scope: Repeated multiplication, initial values, linear comparison, and positive decay bases.

practice.prompt: Start with five and triple twice. List the starting value and both later values.
practice.answer: Five, fifteen, forty five.

practice.prompt: A quantity follows y=80(0.75)^t. Find its value after two steps and describe the percentage retained each step.
practice.answer: 80×0.75²=45; each step retains75%, a25% decrease.

practice.prompt: Compare sequences 4,8,12,16 and 4,8,16,32. Explain which is linear and which is exponential.
practice.answer: The first adds four each step and is linear; the second multiplies by two and is exponential.

lessons.title: Angles and intersecting lines
lessons.objective: Use straight, vertical, and parallel-line angle relationships.

lessons.title: Triangles
lessons.objective: Use angle sums, triangle inequality, and the Pythagorean theorem.

lessons.title: Congruence
lessons.objective: Match corresponding parts and justify congruence with valid criteria.

lessons.title: Similarity
lessons.objective: Use scale factors and distinguish length, area, and volume scaling.

lessons.title: Circles, arcs, and sectors
lessons.objective: Connect radius, circumference, arc length, and sector area.

lessons.title: Area
lessons.objective: Derive triangle, parallelogram, and trapezoid areas by rearranging.

lessons.title: Volume and surface area
lessons.objective: Distinguish boundary area from enclosed volume and use base-area formulas.

lessons.title: Coordinate geometry
lessons.objective: Use distance, midpoint, and slope to justify geometric claims.

lessons.title: Proof basics
lessons.objective: Connect each geometric claim to a definition, given fact, or established result.

lessons.title: Mean, median, and mode
lessons.objective: Calculate measures of center and explain their response to outliers.

lessons.title: Variance
lessons.objective: Calculate squared deviations and distinguish population from sample variance.

lessons.title: Standard deviation
lessons.objective: Interpret spread in the original units and distinguish spread from shape.

lessons.title: Distributions
lessons.objective: Read frequency displays and describe center, spread, skew, and extremes.

lessons.title: Correlation
lessons.objective: Interpret linear association without assuming causation.

lessons.title: Basic probability
lessons.objective: Interpret both, either, and at least one; use complements and changing counts.

lessons.title: Advanced quadratics
lessons.objective: Complete the square and connect vertex form, discriminant, and roots.

lessons.title: Polynomial functions
lessons.objective: Connect degree, leading behavior, zeros, and root multiplicity.

lessons.title: Rational functions
lessons.objective: Simplify common factors while preserving domain restrictions and holes.

lessons.title: Radicals
lessons.objective: Use principal roots, conjugates, and original-equation checks.

lessons.title: Complex numbers
lessons.objective: Use a+bi, complex arithmetic, and multiplication as rotation and scaling.

lessons.title: Exponentials
lessons.objective: Model repeated multiplication with growth and decay factors.

lessons.title: Logarithms
lessons.objective: Interpret logarithms as exponents and apply laws on valid domains.

lessons.title: Sequences
lessons.objective: Distinguish explicit and recursive arithmetic and geometric rules.

lessons.title: Series
lessons.objective: Add finite sequences and determine basic geometric convergence.

lessons.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
lessons.objective: Choose side ratios relative to a marked angle and solve right triangles.
lessons.takeaway: Right-triangle trigonometric ratios depend on the angle, not on triangle size.
lessons.scope: Opposite and adjacent sides, normalization, similarity, and solving a side.

practice.prompt: A right triangle has opposite side eight and hypotenuse seventeen relative to angle A. Find sin A.
practice.answer: sin A=8/17.

practice.prompt: For an acute angle, sin A=5/13 and the hypotenuse is thirty nine. Find the opposite side.
Explain why doubling every side of a right triangle leaves its sine and cosine ratios unchanged.
practice.answer: Each numerator and denominator gets the same factor two, which cancels; the angles and shape remain unchanged.

lessons.title: Sine, cosine, and tangent
lessons.objective: Interpret the three ratios and their reciprocal relationships.
lessons.takeaway: Cosine and sine are coordinates; tangent is their quotient where cosine is nonzero.
lessons.scope: Unit-circle coordinates, exact special values, tangent, and its domain.

practice.prompt: For a unit-circle point (12/13,5/13), state cosine and sine of its angle.
practice.answer: Cosine is12/13 and sine is5/13.

practice.prompt: Using that same point, find tangent and explain its ratio.
practice.answer: tan θ=(5/13)/(12/13)=5/12, vertical coordinate divided by horizontal coordinate.

practice.prompt: Why is tangent undefined when the unit-circle point is (0,−1), while sine is defined?
practice.answer: Tangent divides by the horizontal coordinate zero; sine is simply the defined vertical coordinate−1.

lessons.title: Unit circle
lessons.objective: Read sine and cosine as coordinates with quadrant signs.
lessons.takeaway: Coordinates supply signs, and full turns explain periodicity.
lessons.scope: Angles beyond ninety degrees, quadrant signs, reference angles, and periodicity.

practice.prompt: Give the unit-circle coordinates at angle π radians.
practice.answer: (−1,0), so cosine is−1 and sine is0.

practice.prompt: Find cos(5π/3) and sin(5π/3), explaining their signs.
practice.answer: Cosine is1/2 and sine is−√3/2; the point lies in quadrant IV.

practice.prompt: Explain why angles π/4 and 9π/4 have the same sine and cosine.
practice.answer: They differ by2π, one complete turn, so they end at the same unit-circle point.

lessons.title: Radians
lessons.objective: Measure angles as arc length divided by radius and convert angle units.
lessons.takeaway: Radian measure is arc length divided by radius; arc length equals radius times radians.
lessons.scope: Radian meaning, arc length, full-turn equivalence, and degree conversion.

practice.prompt: Convert forty five degrees to radians, showing the conversion factor.
practice.answer: 45×π/180=π/4 radians.

practice.prompt: A radius-five circle has an arc subtended by 1.4 radians. Find the arc length.
practice.answer: s=rθ=5×1.4=7 length units.

practice.prompt: An arc measures twelve centimeters on a radius-eight-centimeter circle. Find its angle and explain why the radius matters.
practice.answer: θ=s/r=12/8=1.5 radians; the same arc length bends through different angles on different radii.

lessons.title: Trigonometric graphs
lessons.objective: Read amplitude, period, phase, and vertical shifts from periodic graphs.
lessons.takeaway: Output scale changes amplitude; input scale changes period; addition moves the midline.
lessons.scope: Sine cycles, amplitude, period, and vertical shifts.

practice.prompt: State the amplitude and period of y=3cos(x).
practice.answer: Amplitude3 and period2π.

practice.prompt: Find the amplitude, period, and midline of y=4sin(3x)−2.
practice.answer: Amplitude4, period2π/3, midline y=−2.

practice.prompt: A wave ranges from −5 to seven. Find its midline and amplitude, explaining the difference from its full height.
practice.answer: Midline1 and amplitude6; peak-to-trough height is12, twice the amplitude.

lessons.title: Trigonometric identities
lessons.objective: Derive and use identities while preserving domains and every solution.
lessons.takeaway: Identities preserve values on valid domains; cancellation and square roots need conditions.
lessons.scope: Pythagorean identity, structural substitution, cancellations, and quadrant signs.

practice.prompt: If cos θ=7/25, find sin²θ using an identity.
Simplify cos²θ/(1−sin²θ), stating its restriction.
practice.answer: It equals1 where cos θ≠0, since the denominator equals cos²θ.

practice.prompt: If sin θ=8/17 and θ lies in quadrant II, find cos θ and justify the sign.
practice.answer: cos²θ=225/289, so cos θ=−15/17 because quadrant II has negative horizontal coordinates.

lessons.title: Trigonometric equations
lessons.objective: Find all solutions in a specified interval or describe the full periodic family.
lessons.takeaway: Respect the requested interval, include periodic families, and do not divide away zero factors.
lessons.scope: Multiple angles per output, interval solutions, periodic families, and factor preservation.

practice.prompt: Solve cos x=0 for 0≤x<2π.
practice.answer: x=π/2 or3π/2.

practice.prompt: Solve sin x=−√3/2 for 0≤x<2π, explaining the quadrants.
practice.answer: x=4π/3 or5π/3, in quadrants III and IV.

practice.prompt: Solve sin x(2cos x−1)=0 for 0≤x<2π without losing any factors.
practice.answer: sin x=0 gives0,π; cos x=1/2 givesπ/3,5π/3. The four solutions are0,π/3,π,5π/3.

lessons.title: Function transformations
lessons.objective: Explain shifts, stretches, reflections, and order of operations on graphs.
lessons.takeaway: Inside changes alter the input needed; outside changes alter the output produced.
lessons.scope: Horizontal shifts, vertical stretches, vertical shifts, and operation order.

practice.prompt: Describe how y=(x+3)² moves the graph of y=x² and locate the vertex.
practice.answer: It shifts left three; vertex(−3,0).

practice.prompt: For y=−2(x−1)²+4, name the transformations and vertex.
practice.answer: Shift right one, reflect across the horizontal axis and stretch vertically by2, then shift up4; vertex(1,4).

practice.prompt: Explain why f(x−5) moves a graph right rather than left by tracking the old input zero.
practice.answer: To feed zero to f, solve x−5=0, giving the new input x=5. Every old input is reached five units later.

lessons.title: Composite functions
lessons.objective: Track inner and outer inputs and determine a composite function domain.
lessons.takeaway: Compose from the inside out and check that every intermediate output is allowed.
lessons.scope: Function order, evaluation, whole-expression substitution, and composite domains.

practice.prompt: Let f(u)=u−5 and g(x)=4x. Find f(g(2)) with both stages shown.
Using those functions, find g(f(2)) and compare.
practice.answer: f(2)=−3, theng(−3)=−12; the order changes the result.

practice.prompt: Let r(u)=1/u and s(x)=x²−16. State the domain of r(s(x)) and explain both stages.
practice.answer: s accepts every real x, but its output must not be zero. Thus x≠−4 andx≠4.

lessons.title: Inverse functions
lessons.objective: Reverse a one-to-one rule and distinguish an inverse from a reciprocal.
lessons.takeaway: An inverse undoes unique pairings; it is not a reciprocal.
lessons.scope: Undoing linear rules, reflection, injectivity, and domain restrictions.

practice.prompt: Find the inverse of f(x)=5x−4 by undoing its operations.
Check both compositions for f(x)=x+6 and f⁻¹(x)=x−6.
Why does x² need a domain restriction to have an inverse function? Give a valid restriction and inverse.
practice.answer: Inputs a and−a share a², so reversal is ambiguous. Restrict x≥0; then the inverse is√x forx≥0.

lessons.title: Advanced exponentials and logs
lessons.objective: Solve exponential and logarithmic models with valid bases and domains.
lessons.takeaway: Logarithms invert positive-base exponentials; log laws retain every original argument restriction.
lessons.scope: Change of base, exponential solving, logarithm laws, and domain checks.

practice.prompt: Solve 3ˣ=11 using logarithms; an exact expression is sufficient.
State the real domain before simplifying ln(x−2)+ln(x+2).
practice.answer: Both arguments must be positive, sox>2. The sum becomesln(x²−4) only on that original domain.

practice.prompt: Solve ln(x−2)+ln(x+2)=ln(5), checking candidates against the original domain.
practice.answer: x²−4=5 givesx=±3; onlyx=3 lies inx>2.

lessons.title: Parametric equations
lessons.objective: Describe a path with two functions of a shared parameter.
lessons.takeaway: One parameter synchronizes coordinates and preserves direction and timing that a locus alone can lose.
lessons.scope: Shared parameters, evaluation, elimination, circular paths, and traversal speed.

practice.prompt: For x=2t−1 and y=t+4, find the point at t=3.
practice.answer: The point is(5,7).

practice.prompt: Eliminate t from x=t+1 and y=t², keeping the full real parameter domain.
practice.answer: t=x−1, so y=(x−1)² for all realx.

practice.prompt: Compare x=cos t,y=sin t with x=cos t,y=−sin t for increasing t.
practice.answer: Both trace the unit circle, but the first goes counterclockwise and the second clockwise, starting at(1,0).

lessons.title: Polar coordinates
lessons.objective: Translate radius-angle pairs to Cartesian coordinates and interpret repeated representations.
lessons.takeaway: Radius-angle descriptions can be nonunique; conversion requires sign and quadrant awareness.
lessons.scope: Polar-to-Cartesian conversion, full turns, and negative radii.

practice.prompt: Convert polar coordinates (4,π/2) to Cartesian coordinates.
Give one polar description of (−3,0) with a nonnegative radius.
practice.answer: (r,θ)=(3,π), with angles understood modulo2π.

practice.prompt: Show that (−2,0) and (2,π) as polar pairs name the same Cartesian point.

lessons.title: Sequences and series
lessons.objective: Reason about limiting terms, partial sums, and convergence of basic models.
lessons.takeaway: Terms and partial sums are different sequences; vanishing terms alone do not ensure a finite sum.
lessons.scope: Sequence limits, geometric partial sums, and a divergence counterexample.

practice.prompt: List the first four terms of a_n=2/3ⁿ for n starting at one.
Find the sum 1/3+1/9+1/27+… and state why it converges.
practice.answer: It is geometric with first term1/3 and ratio1/3, so the sum is(1/3)/(1−1/3)=1/2 because the ratio magnitude is below one.

practice.prompt: A sequence of terms tends to zero. Does this alone prove their infinite series converges? Explain with a counterexample.
practice.answer: No. Terms1/n tend to zero, but the harmonic series diverges; grouped blocks keep adding at least a fixed positive amount.

lessons.title: Introduction to limits
lessons.objective: Compare function values with the value approached from nearby inputs.
lessons.takeaway: Nearby agreement determines a limit; the point value and the two approaches must be distinguished.
lessons.scope: Removable gaps, valid simplification near a point, and one-sided agreement.

practice.prompt: For f(x)=x+4 except at x=2 where it is undefined, find the limit as x approaches two. Explain.
practice.answer: The nearby rule approaches six, so the limit is6 even though f(2) is undefined.

practice.prompt: Simplify (x²−100)/(x−10) near x=10 and determine its limit there.
practice.answer: Forx≠10 it equalsx+10; asx approaches10 the output approaches20.

practice.prompt: A function approaches three from the left of a point and negative two from the right. Can it have a two-sided limit there?
practice.answer: No. A two-sided limit requires the two one-sided limits to agree.

lessons.title: Limits and simplification
lessons.objective: Evaluate limits by valid algebra near a point while preserving the original domain.
lessons.takeaway: Simplification on nearby allowed inputs can reveal a limit without filling a missing function value.
lessons.scope: First lesson on removable gaps, legal cancellation, and agreement of one-sided limits.

practice.prompt: Find the limit of 5x−4 as x approaches 2. Explain why substitution is valid here.
practice.answer: The polynomial is continuous, so the limit is 5(2)−4=6.

practice.prompt: Find lim x→−2 (x²−4)/(x+2). Show the factorization and keep the original excluded input.
practice.answer: For x≠−2, (x²−4)/(x+2)=(x−2)(x+2)/(x+2)=x−2. The limit is −4; the original is still undefined at −2.

practice.prompt: Let g(x)=3x−2 for x≠1, but g(1)=100. Find the limit at 1 and decide whether g is continuous there.
practice.answer: Nearby outputs approach 1, so the limit is 1. Since g(1)=100, g is not continuous at 1.

lessons.title: Continuity
lessons.objective: Check that a value, a limit, and their agreement all exist at a point.
lessons.takeaway: Continuity requires the nearby limit to equal the function value, with endpoint approaches taken inside the domain.
lessons.scope: Continuity at interior points, removable discontinuities, and a domain endpoint.

practice.prompt: For x≠2, f(x)=(x²−4)/(x−2). What value should f(2) receive to make f continuous? Show why.
practice.answer: For x≠2 the formula equals x+2, whose limit at 2 is 4. Set f(2)=4.

practice.prompt: Is |x| continuous at zero even though it has a corner? Explain using the limit.
practice.answer: Yes. Both sides approach 0, which equals |0|. A corner can prevent differentiability without preventing continuity.

practice.prompt: Can any real choice for f(0) make f(x)=1/x, x≠0, continuous at zero? Explain.
practice.answer: No. There is no finite two-sided limit at zero; the right side grows without bound and the left decreases without bound. A single value cannot repair that behavior.

lessons.title: Derivatives and difference quotients
lessons.objective: Build instantaneous rate from nearby average rates and justify cancellation.
lessons.takeaway: The derivative is a limit of nonzero-input-change quotients; simplify legally before taking the limit.
lessons.scope: Difference quotients, tangent slope, and a continuous function with no derivative at a corner.

practice.prompt: Starting from the difference quotient for f(x)=x² at x=−2, simplify it for h≠0 and find the derivative.
practice.answer: [(-2+h)²−4]/h=(-4h+h²)/h=−4+h for h≠0. The derivative is −4.

practice.prompt: Use expansion to find the derivative of f(x)=x³ at x=1 from [f(1+h)−f(1)]/h.
practice.answer: [(1+h)³−1]/h=(3h+3h²+h³)/h=3+3h+h² for h≠0; the limit is 3.

practice.prompt: Explain why f(x)=|x| can be continuous at zero but have no derivative there. Give the two one-sided slopes.
practice.answer: Both function values approach f(0)=0, so continuity holds. The left slope is −1 and the right slope is +1, so the derivative does not exist.

lessons.title: Product and quotient rules
lessons.objective: Differentiate products and quotients while tracking signs and domain restrictions.
lessons.takeaway: Differentiate the expression's structure, then use algebra to simplify while retaining original exclusions.
lessons.scope: The product rule, quotient rule, and a legal simplification shortcut.

practice.prompt: Differentiate y=x²(x−5), then expand and collect like terms. Name the rule you used.
practice.answer: Product rule: y′=2x(x−5)+x²=3x²−10x.

practice.prompt: Differentiate q(x)=(x+4)/(x+2). Show the subtraction in the numerator and state the domain.
At one point, u=1, u′=2, v=3, and v′=−1. Find both (uv)′ and (u/v)′, explaining why their rules differ.
practice.answer: (uv)′=2·3+1·(−1)=5. (u/v)′=[2·3−1·(−1)]/3²=7/9. A quotient includes the denominator's inverse, producing subtraction and a squared denominator.

lessons.title: Chain rule
lessons.objective: Multiply outer and inner rates for a composition and identify each layer.
lessons.takeaway: Differentiate the outside at the inside, multiply by the inside's derivative, and keep the original domain.
lessons.scope: Two-layer compositions involving powers, roots, and natural logarithms.

practice.prompt: Differentiate (5x−2)³. Identify the inner function and the missing factor someone would lose by using only the power rule.
practice.answer: Inner function u=5x−2 has u′=5. The derivative is 3(5x−2)²·5=15(5x−2)².

practice.prompt: Differentiate √(2+x²), show why a factor of 2 cancels, and state whether x=0 remains allowed.
practice.answer: The derivative is 2x/[2√(2+x²)]=x/√(2+x²). Only the nonzero constant 2 is cancelled. All real x, including 0, remain allowed.

practice.prompt: Compare derivatives of e^(3x) and (e^x)³. Explain why the results must agree.
practice.answer: Both functions equal e^(3x). The first derivative is 3e^(3x) by the chain rule; the second is 3(e^x)²·e^x=3e^(3x).

lessons.title: Implicit differentiation
lessons.objective: Differentiate relations while accounting for y as a function of x.
lessons.takeaway: Treat y as a function of x, apply the chain rule, and justify every division when solving for the slope.
lessons.scope: Implicit differentiation of a circle and interpretation of vertical tangents.

practice.prompt: For x²+y²=25, find dy/dx at (3,4). Show the chain-rule factor.
For xy=6, differentiate implicitly and find the slope at (2,3).
practice.answer: Product rule gives y+x y′=0. Thus y′=−y/x, and the slope at (2,3) is −3/2.

practice.prompt: Explain why differentiating y² with respect to x gives 2y y′ rather than just 2y. What assumption is needed before solving by division by y?
practice.answer: y is a function of x, so the chain rule contributes y′. Dividing by y requires y≠0; points where y=0 must be examined separately.

lessons.title: Optimization
lessons.objective: Model an objective and constraints, compare candidates, and interpret endpoints.
lessons.takeaway: Write the constraint, respect the domain, find candidates, and justify the optimum rather than trusting a zero derivative alone.
lessons.scope: One-variable constrained rectangle optimization with both calculus and completing-the-square justification.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 28. Write its area using one side x, find its maximum, and explain why the answer is a square.
practice.answer: The other side is 14−x, with 0≤x≤14. A=14x−x²=49−(x−7)², so the maximum is 49 at x=7 and y=7.

practice.prompt: Two nonnegative numbers have sum 12. Find their largest possible product and justify the result algebraically or with calculus.
practice.answer: Let them be x and 12−x. Their product is 36−(x−6)²≤36. Equality occurs at 6 and 6.

practice.prompt: The derivative of f(x)=x² is zero at x=0. Explain why this does not make zero a maximum.
practice.answer: f(x)=x²≥0 with equality at 0, so zero is a global minimum. A stationary point can be a minimum, maximum, or neither; classification needs additional reasoning.

lessons.title: Related rates
lessons.objective: Connect rates through a shared equation and substitute at the correct stage.
lessons.takeaway: Differentiate the relationship with respect to time before substituting a particular instant; signs and units explain the answer.
lessons.scope: Area growth and a sliding ladder as two concrete related-rates models.

practice.prompt: A circle's radius is 5 cm and increases at 0.2 cm/s. Find the instantaneous area growth rate, including units.
practice.answer: dA/dt=2πr dr/dt=2π·5·0.2=2π cm²/s.

practice.prompt: A 13 m ladder has its foot 5 m from a wall and its top 12 m high. Its foot moves outward at 3 m/s. Find the top's vertical velocity.
practice.answer: x x′+y y′=0 gives y′=−5·3/12=−5/4 m/s. The negative sign means downward.

practice.prompt: A sphere has V=(4/3)πr³. At r=2 m, dr/dt=0.1 m/s. Derive and calculate dV/dt; explain why r stays a function until differentiation is finished.
practice.answer: dV/dt=4πr² dr/dt=4π·4·0.1=1.6π m³/s. r changes with time; replacing it by the instant's value before differentiating would lose that dependence.

lessons.title: Integrals
lessons.objective: Connect signed accumulation, Riemann sums, and antiderivatives.
lessons.takeaway: Integrals accumulate signed quantities; distance and other totals may require integrating absolute values.
lessons.scope: Constant and variable accumulation, signed area, and the antiderivative constant.

practice.prompt: Find ∫₂⁴ 6 dt and explain the units if 6 is measured in liters per minute and t in minutes.
practice.answer: The integral is 6(4−2)=12 liters. Rate multiplied by elapsed time gives accumulated volume.

practice.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀¹ (3x²+2) dx using an antiderivative and show both endpoint values.
practice.answer: An antiderivative is x³+2x. Evaluating at 1 and 0 gives 3−0=3.

practice.prompt: For v(t)=t−1 on 0≤t≤3, find displacement and total distance. Explain the difference.
practice.answer: Displacement is [t²/2−t]₀³=3/2. Distance is the magnitude of the negative triangular area 1/2 plus the positive area 2, giving 5/2.

lessons.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus
lessons.objective: Connect rates and accumulation under explicit continuity hypotheses.
lessons.takeaway: Differentiation recovers a continuous accumulation rate, and antiderivatives turn definite integrals into endpoint differences.
lessons.scope: Both directions of the fundamental theorem and why continuity matters.

practice.prompt: Use the fundamental theorem to evaluate ∫₂⁴ 3x² dx. Show the antiderivative.
practice.answer: An antiderivative is x³. The integral is 4³−2³=64−8=56.

practice.prompt: If A(x)=∫₀ˣ (t²+1) dt, find A′(x) and A′(2) without first evaluating the integral.
practice.answer: Because the integrand is continuous, A′(x)=x²+1. Therefore A′(2)=5.

practice.prompt: Let B(x)=∫₀^(3x) cos(t) dt. Find B′(x) and explain the extra factor.
practice.answer: The fundamental theorem gives the integrand at the upper limit; the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of 3x. Thus B′(x)=3cos(3x).

lessons.title: Integration techniques
lessons.objective: Select substitution, parts, partial fractions, and trigonometric methods.
lessons.takeaway: Choose substitutions by the chain rule and integration by parts by the product rule; verify antiderivatives by differentiating.
lessons.scope: One substitution pattern, a definite substitution, and a first integration-by-parts example.

practice.prompt: Evaluate ∫3x²(x³+1)² dx by substitution. State u and du, then check by differentiating.
practice.answer: Set u=x³+1, du=3x² dx. The integral is u³/3+C=(x³+1)³/3+C. Its derivative is (x³+1)²·3x².

practice.prompt: Use integration by parts to find ∫x cos(x) dx.
practice.answer: Take u=x and dv=cos x dx, so du=dx and v=sin x. The result is x sin x−∫sin x dx=x sin x+cos x+C.

practice.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 2x(x²+3)² dx by changing the limits to u-values. Explain why the new bounds are 3 and 4.
practice.answer: For u=x²+3, x=0 gives u=3 and x=1 gives u=4. The integral is ∫₃⁴u² du=(64−27)/3=37/3.

lessons.title: Applications of integration
lessons.objective: Build area, volume, work, and average-value integrals with correct bounds and units.
lessons.takeaway: Identify the quantity contributed by one small slice before integrating: height, cross-sectional area, or density.
lessons.scope: Area between curves, disk volume, and mass from a nonuniform density.

practice.prompt: Find the area between y=2x and y=x² on 0≤x≤2. Show which curve is above the other.
practice.answer: 2x−x²=x(2−x)≥0 on [0,2], so area=∫₀²(2x−x²)dx=[x²−x³/3]₀²=4/3.

practice.prompt: Rotate the region under y=√x on 0≤x≤4 about the x-axis. Write the disk integral and compute the volume.
practice.answer: Disk radius is √x, so area is πx. V=∫₀⁴πx dx=8π cubic units.

practice.prompt: A 2 m rod has density 3x+1 kg/m at position x meters from one end. Find its mass and explain the units.
practice.answer: M=∫₀²(3x+1)dx=[3x²/2+x]₀²=8 kg. Density in kg/m multiplied by dx in meters gives kilograms.

lessons.title: Improper integrals
lessons.objective: Replace unbounded intervals or integrands with limits and test convergence.
lessons.takeaway: An improper integral is a limit of ordinary integrals; small heights or unbounded heights alone do not decide convergence.
lessons.scope: An infinite tail, a divergent comparison, and an integrable endpoint singularity.

practice.prompt: Evaluate ∫₁^∞ 3/x² dx by explicitly introducing a finite upper bound R.
practice.answer: ∫₁ᴿ3/x² dx=3−3/R, whose limit as R→∞ is 3.

practice.prompt: Does ∫₁^∞1/√x dx converge? Show the finite-bound expression rather than reasoning only that the integrand approaches zero.
practice.answer: ∫₁ᴿx^(−1/2)dx=2√R−2, which grows without bound. The improper integral diverges.

practice.prompt: Determine whether ∫₀¹1/x² dx converges. Explain which one-sided limit defines it.
practice.answer: Use ε→0+ of ∫ε¹x^(−2)dx=1/ε−1. This diverges to infinity, so the integral does not converge.

lessons.title: Infinite sequences
lessons.objective: Define convergence of sequences and compare growth rates.
lessons.takeaway: Convergence means settling near one value; monotonicity with a bound or a shrinking error can establish it.
lessons.scope: Explicit sequences, oscillation, a monotone convergence example, and a contracting recurrence.

practice.prompt: Find the limit of a_n=(5n+2)/n. Show a simplification that separates the persistent part from the vanishing part.
practice.answer: a_n=5+2/n. Since 2/n→0, the limit is 5.

practice.prompt: Does a_n=(−1)^n/n converge? Explain why alternating signs do not prevent convergence in this case.
practice.answer: Yes, it converges to 0. Its magnitude is 1/n→0, so −1/n≤a_n≤1/n and the squeeze theorem applies.

practice.prompt: Let a_1=4 and a_(n+1)=(a_n+10)/2. Compute the next three terms and justify the limiting value.
practice.answer: The next terms are 7, 8.5, and 9.25. The distance from 10 halves each time, so a_n→10.

lessons.title: Infinite series
lessons.objective: Use partial sums and convergence tests while distinguishing absolute and conditional convergence.
lessons.takeaway: A series converges when its partial sums converge; term size, signs, and valid error conditions all matter.
lessons.scope: Geometric convergence, harmonic divergence, and a controlled alternating approximation.

practice.prompt: Find ∑ from n=0 to infinity of (1/3)^n. State the condition that permits the geometric sum formula.
practice.answer: The ratio is 1/3, whose absolute value is less than 1. The sum is 1/(1−1/3)=3/2.

practice.prompt: Does ∑ from n=1 to infinity of (2n+1)/(n+1) converge? Identify the quickest necessary-condition check.
practice.answer: The terms approach 2, not 0, so the series diverges by the term test.

practice.prompt: For 1−1/2+1/3−1/4+…, bound the magnitude of the error after ten terms. Explain why the bound applies.
practice.answer: The error is at most 1/11 because magnitudes decrease to zero and signs alternate. The next omitted term bounds the alternating-series error.

lessons.title: Taylor series
lessons.objective: Approximate smooth functions locally and analyze interval and error bounds.
lessons.takeaway: Taylor polynomials provide local approximations; remainder bounds and convergence domains determine when they can be trusted.
lessons.scope: The exponential Taylor expansion, a numerical error bound, and a power-series convergence interval.

practice.prompt: Use the degree-two Taylor polynomial of e^x about zero to estimate e^0.1. State the polynomial and the estimate.
The first nonconstant term of the Taylor expansion of cos x is −x²/2. Use its degree-two polynomial to estimate cos(0.2), with angles in radians.
practice.answer: P₂(x)=1−x²/2, so P₂(0.2)=1−0.04/2=0.98. It is a local approximation, not an exact identity.

practice.prompt: Can 1+x+x²+… represent 1/(1−x) at x=1.2? What about x=−0.5? Explain using the ratio.
practice.answer: At 1.2 the terms fail to tend to zero, so the series diverges. At −0.5 the ratio has magnitude below one, so the sum is 1/(1+0.5)=2/3.

lessons.title: Vectors in several dimensions
lessons.objective: Use dot and cross products to describe length, projection, and orientation.
lessons.takeaway: Coordinate rules extend to any finite dimension, but projections must not erase components from calculations.
lessons.scope: Three-dimensional components, length, addition, dot product, and normalization.

practice.prompt: Find the length of v=(2,−1,2), then write a unit vector in the same direction.
practice.answer: The length is √(4+1+4)=3. The unit vector is (2/3,−1/3,2/3). Normalization requires a nonzero vector.

practice.prompt: Add u=(2,0,1) and v=(−1,3,2). Explain why a drawing of only the first two coordinates is incomplete.
practice.answer: u+v=(1,3,3). Its planar projection is (1,3), but that does not include the third component 3.

practice.prompt: Compute the dot product of (1,2,−1) and (2,−1,3). Describe the role of the third coordinates.
practice.answer: The dot product is 1·2+2·(−1)+(−1)·3=−3. The first two contributions cancel, but the third contributes −3.

lessons.title: 3D geometry
lessons.objective: Model lines, planes, surfaces, and space curves with coordinates and vectors.
lessons.takeaway: Equations describe allowed triples; distances, normals, and coordinate slices reveal their geometry.
lessons.scope: Points, distances, planes, a normal vector, and a paraboloid cross-section.

practice.prompt: Find the distance between P=(1,2,3) and Q=(4,2,−1). Show the coordinate differences.
Does (2,−1,1) lie on z=x+y? Give a normal vector to this plane.
practice.answer: Yes, since 1=2+(−1). A normal vector is (−1,−1,1), or any nonzero scalar multiple.

practice.prompt: Write the equation of the sphere centered at the origin with radius 3. Check whether (1,2,2) lies on it.
practice.answer: x²+y²+z²=9. At (1,2,2), 1+4+4=9, so the point lies on the sphere.

lessons.title: Partial derivatives
lessons.objective: Distinguish coordinate rates, directional derivatives, gradients, and differentiability.
lessons.takeaway: A partial derivative freezes the other inputs; rates along a path must account for every moving coordinate.
lessons.scope: Coordinate slices and the distinction between partial and total change along a path.

practice.prompt: For f(x,y)=3x²+2y², find both partial derivatives at (2,−1). Explain which variable stays fixed in each calculation.
practice.answer: f_x=6x, so f_x(2,−1)=12; f_y=4y, so f_y(2,−1)=−4. Hold y fixed for f_x and x fixed for f_y.

practice.prompt: For g(x,y)=x²y³, find g_x and g_y, then evaluate both at (1,2).
practice.answer: g_x=2xy³ and g_y=3x²y². At (1,2), they are 16 and 12 respectively.

practice.prompt: Let f=x²+y² and follow x=t, y=3t. Find df/dt at t=2 and explain why using only f_x would be incomplete.
practice.answer: Along the path f=10t², so df/dt=20t=40 at t=2. Both x and y change; equivalently f_x x′+f_y y′=2t+18t.

lessons.title: Multiple integrals
lessons.objective: Integrate over regions using bounds, changes of variables, and Jacobians.
lessons.takeaway: Integrate small contributions over a stated region; inner variables move while outer variables temporarily remain fixed.
lessons.scope: Iterated integrals over a rectangle and a triangle, with bounds tied to geometry.

practice.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀²∫₀¹(x+2y) dy dx. Show the inner integral before using the outer one.
practice.answer: The inner integral is [xy+y²]₀¹=x+1. Integrating from x=0 to 2 gives [x²/2+x]₀²=4.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has side lengths 2 and 4 with constant density 3 kg per square meter. Express its mass as a double integral and evaluate it.
practice.answer: M=∫₀²∫₀⁴3 dy dx=3·8=24 kg.

practice.prompt: Write and evaluate a double integral for the area of 0≤y≤x≤2. Explain why the upper inner bound is variable.
practice.answer: Area=∫₀²∫₀ˣ1 dy dx=∫₀²x dx=2. For each x, the vertical slice stops at y=x, so its bound changes with x.

lessons.title: Vector fields
lessons.objective: Interpret vector-valued functions through flow, divergence, and curl.
lessons.takeaway: A field assigns a vector to a location; evaluating its components reveals local direction and magnitude.
lessons.scope: Radial, rotational, and constant planar fields as concrete vector-field models.

practice.prompt: For F(x,y)=(x,y), find F(−2,3) and its magnitude.
For G(x,y)=(−y,x), find the vector at (1,−2). Verify that it is perpendicular to the position vector.
practice.answer: G(1,−2)=(2,1). The dot product (1,−2)·(2,1)=2−2=0, so they are perpendicular.

practice.prompt: Compare F(x,y)=(x,y) and H(x,y)=(1,0) at (3,4). Which has greater magnitude there, and does this establish a universal comparison?
practice.answer: F has magnitude 5 and H has magnitude 1, so F is larger there. This is not universal: near the origin F can have magnitude below 1.

lessons.title: Line integrals
lessons.objective: Accumulate scalar or vector quantities along parametrized curves.
lessons.takeaway: Vector line integrals add the field's component along oriented movement; path direction changes the sign.
lessons.scope: Work in constant, rotational, and radial fields, plus the orientation rule.

practice.prompt: For the constant force F=(3,0), compute work along the straight path from (0,0) to (2,0).
practice.answer: Force and displacement align, so work is (3,0)·(2,0)=6. Equivalently integrate 3 dx from 0 to 2.

practice.prompt: For F=(−y,x), compute the line integral around the unit circle counterclockwise, then clockwise.
practice.answer: With r=(cos t,sin t), F(r)=r′ and their dot product is 1, so the counterclockwise integral is 2π. Reversing orientation gives −2π.

practice.prompt: For F=(x,y), parametrize the straight path from (0,0) to (1,2) and compute the work.

lessons.title: Surface integrals
lessons.objective: Integrate over surfaces and connect flux with the divergence and Stokes theorems.
lessons.takeaway: Surface integrals use actual surface area; vector flux additionally depends on an oriented normal component.
lessons.scope: A tilted plane's area factor, constant-density mass, and upward versus downward flux.

practice.prompt: A flat surface of area 6 m² carries constant surface density 4 kg/m². Find its mass and identify the small quantity a surface integral adds.
practice.answer: Mass is 4·6=24 kg. Each small contribution is density times actual surface area, ρ dS.

practice.prompt: For the patch z=x+y above 0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤1, compute its surface area using dS=√3 dx dy.
practice.answer: The projected rectangle has area 2, so surface area=∫₀²∫₀¹√3 dy dx=2√3.

practice.prompt: For the same tilted patch above a unit square and constant field F=(0,0,3), compute upward flux. Explain the effect of choosing the downward normal.
practice.answer: The upward normal is (−1,−1,1)/√3, so F·n=3/√3. Multiplying by dS=√3 dxdy and integrating the unit square gives flux 3. Downward orientation gives −3.

lessons.title: Vectors
lessons.objective: Add, scale, and interpret displacement and linear combinations geometrically.
lessons.takeaway: Vector operations combine directed components; scalar multiplication and dot products connect arithmetic to geometry.
lessons.scope: Planar vectors, addition, scaling, length, and perpendicularity.

practice.prompt: Add u=(−3,1) and v=(2,2). Explain the result as horizontal and vertical displacement.
practice.answer: u+v=(−1,3): one unit left and three units up.

practice.prompt: For u=(1,1) and v=(0,2), compute 2u−v and its length.
Check whether (2,3) and (3,−2) are perpendicular. Explain why your numerical test has a geometric meaning.
practice.answer: Their dot product is 2·3+3·(−2)=0. Since both are nonzero and u·v=||u||||v||cosθ, cosθ=0, so the angle is a right angle.

lessons.title: Matrices
lessons.objective: Represent linear maps, multiply compatibly, and interpret matrix columns.
lessons.takeaway: Matrix columns describe basis images, and matrix multiplication composes compatible transformations in order.
lessons.scope: A geometric shear, vector multiplication, composition order, and dimensions.

practice.prompt: For A=[[1,2],[-1,1]], calculate A(2,1) by combining columns.
practice.answer: 2(1,−1)+1(2,1)=(4,−1). This agrees with the row-by-column calculation.

practice.prompt: A rotation matrix is R=[[0,−1],[1,0]]. Find R(1,0) and R(0,1), then describe the rotation.
practice.answer: The images are (0,1) and (−1,0). This is a counterclockwise quarter-turn about the origin.

practice.prompt: A is 2×3 and B is 3×4. Give the size of AB and explain whether BA is defined.
practice.answer: AB is 2×4 because the inner dimensions 3 match. BA would require 4=2, which is false, so BA is not defined.

lessons.title: Linear systems
lessons.objective: Use row operations to describe consistency, rank, and complete solution sets.
lessons.takeaway: Elimination preserves constraints through reversible operations; geometry and matrix invertibility explain unique, missing, or nonunique solutions.
lessons.scope: Two-variable systems, elimination, and the role of dependent equations.

practice.prompt: Solve 3x+y=8 and x−y=0 by elimination, then verify both equations.
practice.answer: Adding gives 4x=8, so x=2. The second equation gives y=2. Then 3·2+2=8 and 2−2=0.

practice.prompt: Compare the systems u+v=2, 2u+2v=4 and u+v=2, 2u+2v=5. How many solutions does each have?
practice.answer: The first has infinitely many solutions because the second equation repeats the first. The second has none because doubling u+v=2 requires 4, not 5.

practice.prompt: For A=[[1,1],[2,2]] and b=(3,7), explain why Ax=b has no solution without trying arbitrary values of x.
practice.answer: The second row output is always twice the first. If the first is 3, the second must be 6, never 7. The target is outside the image of A.

lessons.title: Vector spaces
lessons.objective: Use subspaces, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
lessons.takeaway: A vector space is defined by algebraic closure and structure, not by whether its objects look like arrows.
lessons.scope: A line through the origin, a nonexample, and polynomials as vectors.

practice.prompt: Show that S={(x,y):x+y=0} is a subspace of R². Give a spanning vector.
practice.answer: Every member is t(1,−1). The zero vector corresponds to t=0, and adding or scaling multiples gives another multiple. Thus S is a subspace spanned by (1,−1).

practice.prompt: Why is the set of points y=2x+1 not a vector subspace? Give one decisive test and one numerical failure of addition.
practice.answer: It omits (0,0). Also (0,1) lies in the set but adding it to itself gives (0,2), which does not satisfy y=2x+1.

practice.prompt: Represent p(x)=1+x and q(x)=2−x by coefficient vectors. Add them and explain why polynomials of degree exactly one would not form a vector space.
practice.answer: The vectors are (1,1) and (2,−1), adding to (3,0), the constant polynomial 3. Degree exactly one excludes this sum and the zero polynomial, so it fails closure and the zero-vector requirement.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues
lessons.objective: Find scalars associated with invariant directions and solve characteristic equations.
lessons.takeaway: Eigenvalues are the scalings of nonzero eigenvectors; singularity of A−λI identifies the possible values.
lessons.scope: Diagonal examples, the characteristic equation, and a zero eigenvalue.

practice.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of A=[[3,0],[0,−2]] by considering its action on the coordinate axes.
practice.answer: The eigenvalues are 3 and −2. The first axis is stretched by 3, and the second is scaled by −2, reversing direction and doubling length.

practice.prompt: For A=[[1,0],[0,0]], give a nonzero eigenvector with eigenvalue zero. Explain why the zero vector itself is not an eigenvector.
practice.answer: v=(0,1) satisfies Av=(0,0)=0v. The definition excludes v=0, which would otherwise satisfy Av=λv for every scalar and identify no direction.

practice.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of A=[[2,1],[0,2]] using det(A−λI). Must there be two different eigenvalues?
practice.answer: The determinant is (2−λ)², so λ=2 is the only distinct eigenvalue, with algebraic multiplicity two. A 2×2 matrix need not have two distinct eigenvalues.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors
lessons.objective: Find invariant directions and connect diagonalization to repeated transformations.
lessons.takeaway: Solve (A−λI)v=0 for nonzero vectors; an eigenvector basis turns a transformation into independent scalings.
lessons.scope: Two eigenspaces of a symmetric 2×2 matrix and decomposition into eigendirections.

practice.prompt: For A=[[3,1],[1,3]], check whether v=(1,1) is an eigenvector and identify its eigenvalue.
practice.answer: Av=(4,4)=4v, so v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 4.

practice.prompt: For the same matrix, check v=(1,−1). Compare its eigenvalue with the previous direction.
practice.answer: Av=(2,−2)=2v, so its eigenvalue is 2. The two independent directions scale differently.

practice.prompt: For D=[[2,0],[0,5]], explain why (1,1) is not an eigenvector, then compute D(3,−1) using the two coordinate eigendirections.
practice.answer: D(1,1)=(2,5) is not one scalar multiple of (1,1). Decompose (3,−1)=3e₁−e₂; the image is 3·2e₁−5e₂=(6,−5).

lessons.title: Logic
lessons.objective: Use propositions, connectives, quantifiers, and truth conditions precisely.
lessons.takeaway: Distinguish an implication, its converse, and its equivalent contrapositive; a universal claim can be defeated by one counterexample.
lessons.scope: Implication and quantifiers through integer divisibility.

practice.prompt: Prove that an integer divisible by 6 is divisible by 3. Use an arbitrary integer rather than only an example.
practice.answer: If n=6k for integer k, then n=3(2k), and 2k is an integer. Thus 3 divides n.

practice.prompt: Is the converse, 'divisible by 3 implies divisible by 6,' valid? Supply a counterexample if not.
practice.answer: No. The integer 3 is divisible by 3 but not by 6.

practice.prompt: Negate the statement 'For every integer n, n²≥0.' Explain why changing 'every' matters, and state whether the negation is true.
practice.answer: Its negation is 'There exists an integer n with n²<0.' Negating a universal statement requires an existential counterexample, not another universal statement. This negation is false over the integers.

lessons.title: Sets
lessons.objective: Use membership, inclusion, unions, intersections, products, and functions.
lessons.takeaway: Set operations combine membership conditions; overlap and the chosen universe determine the correct counts.
lessons.scope: Membership, intersection, union, disjointness, difference, and a relative complement.

practice.prompt: For A={2,4,6} and B={4,6,8}, find A∩B and A∪B. Check the union size by inclusion-exclusion.
Using those sets, find A\B. Explain why it differs from the intersection.
practice.answer: A\B={2}, keeping elements in A that are not in B. The intersection instead keeps the shared elements 4 and 6.

practice.prompt: Let U={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} and A={2,4,6}. Find the complement of A in U and explain why specifying U is necessary.
practice.answer: U\A={1,3,5,7,8}. Changing the universe changes which nonmembers are available, so a complement is relative to U.

lessons.title: Proofs
lessons.objective: Build direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction arguments.
lessons.takeaway: A proof uses general reasoning under stated assumptions; induction needs both a base case and a valid forward step.
lessons.scope: A direct parity proof, counterexamples, and one induction argument.

practice.prompt: Prove that the sum of two odd integers is even, using arbitrary integer variables.
practice.answer: Write the odd integers as 2a+1 and 2b+1. Their sum is 2(a+b+1), which is even because a+b+1 is an integer.

practice.prompt: Disprove the claim 'Every prime number is odd.' Explain why one example is sufficient here but not sufficient to prove a universal claim.
practice.answer: 2 is prime and even, so it contradicts the universal claim. A universal claim fails if even one allowed object violates it; finitely many positive examples do not establish all cases.

practice.prompt: Prove 1+3+…+(2n−1)=n² by induction. State both the base case and the induction step.
practice.answer: At n=1, 1=1². If the sum through 2n−1 is n², adding the next odd number 2n+1 gives n²+2n+1=(n+1)². Thus the claim holds for all positive integers.

lessons.title: Combinatorics
lessons.objective: Count using sums, products, permutations, combinations, and inclusion-exclusion.
lessons.takeaway: Identify stages, order, and repetition before counting; divide only when you know exactly how many times each outcome was counted.
lessons.scope: The product rule, ordered choices, combinations, and repeated symbols.

practice.prompt: How many ordered arrangements of three different books can be chosen from five different books? Explain each factor.
practice.answer: There are 5 choices first, 4 second, and 3 third, so 5·4·3=60.

practice.prompt: How many three-book groups can be chosen from those five books if order does not matter? Explain the division.
practice.answer: Each group has 3!=6 orderings, so the count is 60/6=10.

practice.prompt: How many four-digit codes use digits 0–9 if repetition and leading zero are allowed? How would excluding repeated digits change the result?
practice.answer: With repetition there are 10⁴=10,000 codes. Without repetition, there are 10·9·8·7=5,040.

lessons.title: Graph theory
lessons.objective: Reason about vertices, edges, paths, trees, and connectivity.
lessons.takeaway: Graph structure records connections; degree, reachability, edge count, and weighted cost answer different questions.
lessons.scope: Undirected graphs, degrees, paths, and the distinction between weighted and unweighted shortest routes.

practice.prompt: In a triangle graph with edges AB, BC, and CA, list the degrees and verify the degree-sum identity.
practice.answer: Each of the three vertices has degree 2. The degree sum is 6=2·3, twice the number of edges.

practice.prompt: Suppose AB has cost 2, BC cost 1, and AC cost 5. Find the least-cost route from A to C and compare it with the route using the fewest edges.
practice.answer: A→B→C costs 3 and is least-cost. The direct A→C edge uses only one edge but costs 5.

practice.prompt: A graph has only edges AB and CD. Is there a path from A to D? Explain using connected components.
practice.answer: No. The vertices form two components {A,B} and {C,D}; no edge connects them.

lessons.title: Algorithms
lessons.objective: Specify procedures and justify correctness, termination, and complexity.
lessons.takeaway: An algorithm needs justified steps, a correctness invariant, and termination; efficiency depends on its assumptions.
lessons.scope: Binary search as a concrete example of algorithm design, correctness, and logarithmic work.

practice.prompt: Use binary search to find 11 in [1,3,5,7,9,11,13]. State each middle comparison.
practice.answer: Compare with 7, then keep [9,11,13]. Its middle is 11, so the target is found after two comparisons.

practice.prompt: Why is ordinary binary search invalid on [9,1,7,3,5]? Use target 3 and the middle value 7 to explain the failure.
practice.answer: The list is unsorted. Comparing 3<7 would discard the right side, but the target 3 is on that discarded side. Sorted order is needed for the elimination rule.

practice.prompt: Starting with 1,024 candidates, how many remain after ten exact halvings? Does this by itself prove that an arbitrary search procedure is correct?
practice.answer: 1,024/2¹⁰=1 remains. No: correctness also needs an invariant ensuring the target was never discarded and a valid stopping rule, possibly including a final comparison.

lessons.title: Counting outcomes
lessons.objective: Choose an equally likely sample space and use combinatorial counting carefully.
lessons.takeaway: Count equally likely underlying outcomes, and update the sample space when earlier choices remove possibilities.
lessons.scope: Dice counting, unequal grouped outcomes, and two draws without replacement.

practice.prompt: List the equally likely outcomes of two independent fair coin tosses. Find the probability of exactly one head.
practice.answer: HH, HT, TH, TT each have probability 1/4. Exactly one head occurs in HT or TH, giving 2/4=1/2.

practice.prompt: Find the probability that two independent fair dice have sum 4. List the favorable ordered pairs.
practice.answer: The pairs are (1,3), (2,2), and (3,1). The probability is 3/36=1/12.

practice.prompt: A bag has five marked and three plain objects. Draw two without replacement. Find the probability both are marked and explain the changed denominator.
practice.answer: (5/8)(4/7)=20/56=5/14. The second denominator is 7 because one object has been removed.

lessons.title: Conditional probability
lessons.objective: Restrict the sample space and distinguish conditional probability from independence.
lessons.takeaway: Condition on the correct group, and test independence instead of assuming probabilities can always be multiplied.
lessons.scope: Conditional denominators, reversed conditions, and the independence criterion.

practice.prompt: Among 20 students, 12 walk to school, 8 cycle, and 3 sometimes do both. Find P(cycle|walk) and P(walk|cycle).
practice.answer: P(cycle|walk)=3/12=1/4. P(walk|cycle)=3/8. The different conditioning groups give different denominators.

practice.prompt: A bag has two green and three purple objects. Given that the first draw was green and was not replaced, find the probability the next draw is green.
practice.answer: One green remains among four objects, so the conditional probability is 1/4.

practice.prompt: Suppose P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and P(A∩B)=0.2. Are A and B independent? Verify with a conditional probability.
practice.answer: Yes: P(A)P(B)=0.2 equals the overlap. Also P(B|A)=0.2/0.4=0.5=P(B), with P(A)>0.

lessons.title: Bayes theorem
lessons.objective: Reverse a conditional probability using base rates and total probability.
lessons.takeaway: To reverse a conditional probability, combine the relevant likelihoods with the base rates and normalize within the observed group.
lessons.scope: Bayes' theorem through a transparent frequency model and a base-rate change.

practice.prompt: Type A accounts for 30% of objects. A rule flags 80% of A and 10% of non-A. Find P(A|flag) using frequencies out of 1,000.
practice.answer: There are 300 A, of which 240 are flagged, and 700 non-A, of which 70 are flagged. P(A|flag)=240/310=24/31≈0.7742.

practice.prompt: Repeat the calculation when A accounts for only 10%, the A flagging rate is 80%, and the non-A flagging rate is 20%.
practice.answer: Out of 1,000, 80 A and 180 non-A are flagged. P(A|flag)=80/260=4/13≈0.3077.

practice.prompt: Explain why '80% of A objects get flagged' does not by itself tell us the percentage of flagged objects that are A. Identify the missing information.
practice.answer: It describes P(flag|A), not P(A|flag). We also need the base rate P(A) and the flagging rate among non-A, which determine the full flagged group.

lessons.title: Random variables
lessons.objective: Map outcomes to values and distinguish discrete mass from continuous density.
lessons.takeaway: A random variable is a numerical function of outcomes, and its distribution groups the probabilities of outcomes sharing a value.
lessons.scope: A coin-count variable, an indicator, transformed values, and events involving a variable.

practice.prompt: Roll a fair die and define X=1 if the face exceeds 4, otherwise X=0. Find the distribution of X.
practice.answer: X=1 for faces 5 and 6, so P(X=1)=1/3. The other four faces give P(X=0)=2/3.

practice.prompt: For three independent fair coin tosses, let X count heads. Find P(X=0) and P(X=3), and identify the underlying outcomes.
practice.answer: TTT gives zero heads and HHH gives three. Each has probability (1/2)³=1/8.

practice.prompt: For X counting heads in two fair independent tosses, define Y=3X+2. List Y's possible values and their probabilities.
practice.answer: Y takes values 2, 5, 8 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 respectively. Each value follows from applying the rule to X=0,1,2.

lessons.title: Probability distributions
lessons.objective: Use Bernoulli, binomial, normal, and other models with explicit assumptions.
lessons.takeaway: Discrete probabilities are masses; continuous probabilities are areas under a density, with assumptions defining the model.
lessons.scope: Discrete probability mass, a binomial example, and uniform continuous density.

practice.prompt: A discrete variable takes values 0,1,2 with probabilities 0.1,0.25,0.65. Verify that this is a valid distribution and find P(X≥1).
practice.answer: All probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1. P(X≥1)=0.25+0.65=0.9.

practice.prompt: Four independent fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of exactly one head, explaining the number of supporting outcomes.
practice.answer: The head can occupy any of four positions, each outcome having probability 1/16. The probability is 4/16=1/4.

practice.prompt: X is uniform on [0,5]. Find its density, P(1≤X≤3), and P(X=2). Explain why the last two answers differ.
practice.answer: Density is 1/5. The interval has length 2, so its probability is 2/5. A single point has zero width and probability 0; density at that point is not its probability.

lessons.title: Expectation
lessons.objective: Calculate weighted averages, variance, and linearity without requiring independence.
lessons.takeaway: Expectation is a weighted average with linearity, not a prediction of a single outcome or a measure of its risk.
lessons.scope: A finite payoff distribution, linearity, and the difference between expected and individual outcomes.
